summary: Proposes a way around the race condition in the Initial Connection Protocol described in RFC 143. The Host-Host protocol did not say what to do with several requests to the same socket, so implementations differ. The suggestion is to fix it in a third-level protocol rather than change the Host-Host protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC addresses a conflict that could occur while two hosts set up an Initial Connection Protocol connection. It proposes using separate sockets for the setup messages so the requests do not target the same socket.

subtitle: A socket arrangement intended to avoid conflicting ICP connection requests.

tldr.problem: The Host-Host protocol did not say how an NCP should handle multiple STR or RTS requests for the same socket, so implementations differed.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal uses different sockets for the two INIT exchanges in the Initial Connection Protocol, rather than changing the Host-Host protocol.
tldr.outcome: The author says this avoids reliance on implementation-specific request handling or NCP notifications.

sections.title: The Socket Request Conflict
sections.content:
RFC 143 described a race condition in the Initial Connection Protocol. The Host-Host protocol did not specify what an NCP should do when it received more than one STR or RTS request for the same socket.

As a result, implementations could behave differently. SDC might queue requests, while UCLA might refuse a request if the socket was already connected.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol left an important case undefined. Different host software could queue a second request or refuse it, so the same connection attempt could behave differently.

sections.title: Use Separate Sockets for INIT
sections.content:
The proposal leaves the Host-Host protocol unchanged and moves the solution into the third-level ICP. It assigns separate sockets, suggested as U+2 and U+3, for the INIT messages between server and user.

Because the two setup exchanges use different sockets, they do not compete for the same socket. The RFC includes the corresponding server and user command sequence from RFC 143.
sections.plainLanguage: The user and server send their setup messages on separate sockets. This avoids the conflict without changing the lower-level protocol.

sections.title: No NCP Notification Assumption
sections.content: The RFC says the proposed arrangement solves the problem without assumptions about how the NCP handles simultaneous requests. It contrasts this with another solution that assumes an NCP can notify a process when a command, such as a close, arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed fix does not depend on the NCP sending a special notice to a process. It avoids the contested behavior by assigning separate sockets.
